'''''Suaeda vera''''', also known as '''shrubby sea-blite''',<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17 }}</ref><ref name=AtlasBrit>{{cite web| title= ''Suaeda vera'' (Shrubby Sea-blite) | work= Online Atlas of the British and Irish Flora | url=http://www.brc.ac.uk/plantatlas/index.php?q=plant/suaeda-vera | publisher= Biological Records Centre }} Retrieved 29 June 2012</ref> '''shrubby seablight'''<ref>[http://www.pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Suaeda+fruticosa Suaeda fruticosa – Forssk.]</ref> or in the US sometimes as '''alkali seepweed''',<ref>{{PLANTS|id=SUVE2|taxon=Suaeda vera|access-date=4 December 2015}}</ref> is a species of [[flowering plant]] in the [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] [[Amaranthaceae]] (formerly classified under the [[Chenopodiaceae]]). It is a small shrub, with very variable appearance over its wide range. It is a [[halophyte]], and occurs in arid and semi-arid saltflats, salt marshes and similar [[habitat]]s.

==Taxonomy==
This species was first [[Species description|described]] according to the modern Linnaean system of taxonomy by [[Linnaeus]] himself in 1753, who called the species ''Chenopodium fruticosum''. A student of his, [[Peter Forsskål]], joined an expedition undertaking a scientific exploration of Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Yemen and further in 1760. Only one explorer survived the journey, but Forsskål's journal and notes made it safely back to Copenhagen, and in 1775 his new data was summarised by the last remaining member of the expedition. Forsskål named a number of ''[[Suaeda]]'' species from the region, including ''S. vera'', [[Suaeda vermiculata|''S. vermiculata'']] and [[Suaeda fruticosa|''S. fruticosa'']],<ref name=Ibérica>{{cite book |last1=Pedrol |first1=J. |last2=Castroviejo |first2=S. |date=1990 |title=Flora Ibérica |volume=II |url=http://www.floraiberica.es/floraiberica/texto/pdfs/02_052_19_Suaeda.pdf |location=Madrid |publisher=Real Jardín Botánico de Madrid |pages=538, 539 |language=es }}</ref> but the 1775 work was not validly published and therefore the names [[nom. inval.|''nomima invalida'']]. In 1776 Forsskål's new genus ''Suaeda'' was validated by [[Johann Friedrich Gmelin]],<ref name=ipni>{{Cite web |title=''Suaeda vera'' Forssk. |url=https://www.ipni.org/n/167587-1 |website=[[International Plant Names Index]] |publisher=The Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, Harvard University Herbaria & Libraries and Australian National Botanic Gardens |access-date=19 October 2020}}</ref> and in 1791 Gmelin validated the species.<ref name=ipni2>{{Cite web |title=''Suaeda vera'' Forssk. ex J.F.Gmel. (1791) |url=https://www.ipni.org/n/167588-1 |website=[[International Plant Names Index]] |publisher=The Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, Harvard University Herbaria & Libraries and Australian National Botanic Gardens |access-date=19 October 2020}}</ref> However, what Forsskål called ''S. vera'' was the same as Linnaeus's ''Chenopodium fruticosum'', whereas what Forsskål called ''S. fruticosa'' was a species that does not occur in Europe, the Near East or North Africa. Nonetheless, the identities were switched, such that ''S. fruticosa'', with the incorrect authority attribution <small>(L.) Forssk.</small> was and still is commonly used across the region,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Schenk |first1=H. Jochen |last2=Ferren |first2=Wayne R. Jr. |date=1 August 2001 |title=On the sectional nomenclature of ''Suaeda'' (Chenopodiaceae) |journal=Taxon |volume=50 |issue=3 |pages=857–873 |doi=10.2307/1223715 |jstor=1223715 |issn=0040-0262}}</ref><ref name=EuroMed>{{cite web |url=https://ww2.bgbm.org/EuroPlusMed/PTaxonDetail.asp?NameId=17986&PTRefFk=7300000 |title=Details for: ''Suaeda vera'' |last=Uotila |first=Petteri |date=2011 |website=EUR+MED flora project |publisher=[[Berlin Botanical Garden and Botanical Museum|Botanic Garden and Botanical Museum Berlin-Dahlem]] |access-date=18 October 2020}}</ref> although the switched identity was discovered in the mid-20th century.<ref name=Dandy1969>{{cite journal |last=Dandy |first=James Edgar |author-link=James Edgar Dandy |date=1969 |title=Nomenclatural changes in the list of British vascular plants |url=http://archive.bsbi.org.uk/Wats7p157.pdf#5 |journal=Watsonia |volume=7 |issue=3 |page=161 |access-date=18 October 2020}}</ref>

William Forsyth Jr. translated Gmelin's 1791 thirteenth edition of the ''[[Systema Naturae]]'' into English as ''A Botanical nomenclator'' in 1794, but decided to move this species to ''Salsola vera'' in his translation, and gives Gmelin's 1776 work as the publication of the [[basionym]], further confusing the issue.<ref name=ipni3>{{Cite web |title=''Suaeda vera'' Forssk. ex J.F.Gmel. (1776) |url=https://www.ipni.org/n/1013554-1 |website=[[International Plant Names Index]] |publisher=The Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, Harvard University Herbaria & Libraries and Australian National Botanic Gardens |access-date=19 October 2020}}</ref>

Another name and taxon tangled up in this confusion is ''S. vermiculata''. According to Petteri Uotila, writing for the ''EUR+MED flora project'' in 2011, this is a species which is only found in Europe in Spain and Sicily, and is otherwise distributed in Africa, four of the Canary Islands, and the Middle East.<ref name=EuroMed/> The ''African Plants Database'' agrees with Uotila that ''S. fruticosa'' does not occur in Africa, but states that the name was misapplied to populations of ''S. vermiculata'' in Africa, not to ''S. vera'', while listing the same works.<ref name=APD>{{cite book|url=http://www.ville-ge.ch/musinfo/bd/cjb/africa/details.php?langue=an&id=26365|title=''Suaeda vermiculata''|publisher=[[Conservatory and Botanical Garden of the City of Geneva]]|work=African Plant Database|access-date=20 October 2020}}</ref> The Database does agree that ''S. vera'' occurs in the Maghreb, and also gives ''S. fruticosa'' as a synonym, but ''S. fruticosa'' under a different authority attribution!<ref name=APD2>{{cite book|url=http://www.ville-ge.ch/musinfo/bd/cjb/africa/details.php?langue=an&id=131918|title=''Suaeda vera''|publisher=[[Conservatory and Botanical Garden of the City of Geneva]]|work=African Plant Database|access-date=20 October 2020}}</ref>

G. Tutin's ''Flora Europaea'' (last edition in 1993) uses the name ''S. fruticosa'' for this taxon.<ref name=EuroMed/>

===Britain===
The British botanist [[Clive A. Stace]] uses the name ''S. fruticosa'' for this species in his ''New Flora of the British Isles''.<ref name=Stace>{{cite book|last=Stace|first=C. A.|author-link = Stace, C. A.|year=2010|title=New Flora of the British Isles|edition=Third|publisher=Cambridge University Press|location = Cambridge, U.K.| isbn=978-0-521-70772-5}}</ref>{{rp|495}} This usage was also found in the 1958 ''List of British Vascular Plants'' by [[James Edgar Dandy]], but in 1969 Dandy corrected the nomenclature to ''S. vera''.<ref name=Dandy1969/> Other British authorities use the name ''S. vera''.<ref name=BSBI07/><ref name=AtlasBrit/>

===Iraq and Israel===
The 2016 ''Flora of Iraq'' accepts ''S. fruticosa'' and ''S. vermiculata'' in the flora of Iraq, but not ''S. vera''.<ref name=PoWO>{{cite web |title=''Suaeda vera'' Forssk. ex J.F.Gmel. |date=2017 |work=[[Plants of the World Online]] |publisher=[[Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew]] |url=http://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/167588-1 |access-date=20 October 2020}}</ref><ref name=PoWO2>{{cite web |title=''Suaeda vermiculata'' Forssk. ex J.F.Gmel. |date=2017 |work=[[Plants of the World Online]] |publisher=[[Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew]] |url=http://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/167589-1 |access-date=20 October 2020}}</ref><ref name=PoWO3>{{cite web |title=''Suaeda fruticosa'' Forssk. ex J.F.Gmel. |date=2017 |work=[[Plants of the World Online]] |publisher=[[Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew]] |url=http://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/247757-2 |access-date=20 October 2020}}</ref> One of the only botanical authorities to recognise all three taxa within the country are Avinoam Danin and Ori Fragman-Sapir in Israel. According to them, all three taxa are valid species and each has a different habitat, with ''S. vera'' occurring along the Mediterranean coast and in the highlands of the central [[Negev Desert]],<ref name=FloraIsrael>{{cite web |url=https://flora.org.il/en/plants/SUAVER/ |title=''Suaeda vera'' Forssk. ex J.F.Gmel. |last1=Danin |first1=Avinoam |last2=Fragman-Sapir |first2=Ori |date=2019 |website=Flora of Israel Online |publisher=Avinoam Danin |access-date=21 October 2020}}</ref> ''S. fruticosa'' occurring around the shores of the [[Dead Sea]],<ref name=FloraIsrael3>{{cite web |url=https://flora.org.il/en/plants/SUAFRU/ |title=''Suaeda fruticosa'' Forssk. ex J.F.Gmel. |last1=Danin |first1=Avinoam |last2=Fragman-Sapir |first2=Ori |date=2019 |website=Flora of Israel Online |publisher=Avinoam Danin |access-date=21 October 2020}}</ref> and with ''S. vermiculata'' in the valley of [[Arabah]].<ref name=FloraIsrael2>{{cite web |url=https://flora.org.il/en/plants/SUAVEM/ |title=''Suaeda vermiculata'' J.F.Gmel. |last1=Danin |first1=Avinoam |last2=Fragman-Sapir |first2=Ori |date=2019 |website=Flora of Israel Online |publisher=Avinoam Danin |access-date=20 October 2020}}</ref> A further complication is that according to the ''Suaeda'' specialist Helmut Freitag in the 2001 ''Flora of Pakistan'', the ''S. vermiculata'' in the 1966 ''Flora Palestina'' by [[Daniel Zohary]] is misidentified, and is actually ''S. fruticosa''.<ref name=Pakistan>{{cite book |last=Freitag |first=Helmut |chapter=Chenopodiaceae: ''Suaeda'' |chapter-url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=5&taxon_id=242100197 |date=2001 |title=Flora of Pakistan |volume=204 |location=Karachi |publisher=University of Karachi }}</ref>

===Spain and Portugal===
The name ''Suaeda vera'' was itself misapplied to a collection of ''S. vermiculata'', which was reported in error in Portugal.<ref name=EuroMed2>{{cite web |url=https://ww2.bgbm.org/EuroPlusMed/PTaxonDetail.asp?NameId=44843&PTRefFk=7300000 |title=Details for: ''Suaeda vermiculata'' |last=Uotila |first=Petteri |date=2011 |website=EUR+MED flora project |publisher=Botanic Garden and Botanical Museum Berlin-Dahlem |access-date=20 October 2020}}</ref> In the 1990 volume of the ''[[Flora Ibérica]]'', only ''S. vera'' was stated to occur in Spain, not ''S. vermiculata'' or ''S. fruticosa''.<ref name=Ibérica/> The ''EUR+MED flora project'' has both ''S. vera'' and ''S. vermiculata'' occurring in Spain, but not ''S. fruticosa''.<ref name=EuroMed/><ref name=EuroMed2/>

==Description==
It has a chromosome number of 2n=36.<ref name=Stace/><ref name=Chapman/>

==Distribution==
The range of this species is primarily along the coasts of the Mediterranean region. In Europe the range extends northwards along the Atlantic coasts of Spain, Portugal, France to south-eastern England. It does not extend around the Black Sea.<ref name=EuroMed/>

Because of the taxonomic confusion, the distribution in Africa is somewhat more complicated. It occurs in the Canary Islands, the [[Maghreb]] countries of northern Africa,<ref name=EuroMed/> and likely into the [[Sahel]] countries of Sudan and Mauritania,<ref name=APD2/> but it is unclear if the populations further in southern Africa, formerly classified as ''Suaeda fruticosa'', belong to ''S. vera'' or ''S. vermiculata''.<ref name=APD/><ref name=APD2/> For example, the 1988 ''Atlas Florae Europaeae'', which is based on an older edition of the ''[[Flora Europaea]]'', includes Cape Verde for ''S. fruticosa'', which this population is not, but it is not clear to which taxon it actually belongs.<ref name=AFE>{{cite book |first1=Jaako |last1=Jalas |first2=Juha |last2=Suominen |date=1988 |title=Atlas Florae Europaeae |volume=2 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=0-521-34271-6}}</ref>{{rp|72}}

In Asia it appears that this species is limited to around the Mediterranean region in the Levant and along the coasts of southern Anatolia.<ref name=EuroMed/><ref name=FloraIsrael/> It does not extend eastwards into Iraq or Pakistan, here the '''real''' ''S. fruticosa'' occurs.<ref name=Pakistan/> A similar situation seems to exist on the Arabian Peninsula.

==Ecology==
Seeds germinate more readily in fresh than in salt water.<ref name=Chapman>{{cite journal |last=Chapman |first=V.J. |date=1947 |title=Biological Flora of the British Isles No. 21: ''Suaeda fruticosa'' Forsk. (''vera'' J.F. Gmelin)|journal=Journal of Ecology |volume=35 |pages=303–310 | doi = 10.2307/2256519|jstor=2256519 }}</ref>{{rp|309}} In Britain it is a coastal species found particularly where shingle and [[salt marsh]] meet.<ref name=AtlasBrit/>

==Uses==
It is one of a number of plants high in sodium known as '[[barilla]]' which were used to make [[Sodium carbonate|soda ash]] for use in the soap and glass industries. Large quantities were exported from North Africa in the 18th and 19th centuries.<ref name="Wickens">{{cite book|author1=Wickens, G.E.|author2=Field, David. V.|author3=Goodin, Joe R.|title=Plants for Arid Lands: Proceedings of the Kew International Conference on Economic Plants for Arid Lands held in the Jodrell Laboratory, Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, England, 23–27 July 1984|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=XD7sCAAAQBAJ&pg=PA181 |year=2012 |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media|isbn=978-94-011-6830-4 |page=181}}</ref> In a trial in Tunisia it has been found possible to grow both ''Suaeda'' and the cordgrass ''[[Spartina alterniflora]]'' using seawater to irrigate them and increase yields, but only when additional nitrogen and phosphorus are added. The high salt content of the plants will be likely to limit their use as stand alone forage crops, it being more likely they will be used as components of a feed mix.<ref>{{cite book|author1=Ahmad, R.|author2=Malik, K.A.|title=Prospects for Saline Agriculture |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=6s3rCAAAQBAJ&pg=PA404 |year=2013 |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |isbn=978-94-017-0067-2 |pages=404–408}}</ref>
